meaning.evidence: Every guideline survives: 40 °F, frozen meat packed, separate drinks esky, limit opening, wrap raw meat, rinse produce including rinds, ready-to-eat exception, hand cleaning, marinade in fridge and reserve a portion, partial cooking, thermometer, keep hot at the side, clean platter.

sense.evidence: Mostly exact ("Stick cold food in an esky", "kitchen bench", "tea towel", "rocked up"), but "gives the nasty bugs in your tucker a real chance to go off" uses "go off" (spoil, or explode) for bacteria thriving, and "out in the bush too" narrows "outdoor settings".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Aussie telling you: "copping a dose of food poisoning", "dead important", "the perishables aren't copping the warm outside air", "cooked to buggery".

register.evidence: Level 4 throughout, with dad-level swearing only ("bloody rabbits", "to buggery").

tone.evidence: Stays a practical safety guide under the slang; the rules stay rules ("Don't reuse marinade.").

flow.evidence: Reads well; "Meat, chook and seafood" repeated four times and "there's some important rules" are slightly clunky.

variety.evidence: Good spread ("barbie", "tucker", "esky", "chook", "mates", "lugging", "rocked up", "dead important"), though "chook" and "esky" recur by necessity.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the FDA guide with its sections and headings intact.

problems.quote: gives the nasty bugs in your tucker a real chance to go off
problems.original: present opportunities for foodborne bacteria to thrive
problems.why: "go off" means food spoiling or something exploding, not bacteria thriving; muddles the sense.
Colloquial agreement slip; acceptable in speech but a little rough.

A.summary: A faithful, natural level-4 guide; a couple of slightly loose terms.

meaning.evidence: All points kept, with colour that hangs off the original ("Snags burnin' and the flies havin' a go", "Guessing doesn't count", "every five minutes") and a helpful "(about 4 °C)" beside 40 °F. "a nasty dose of the runs" narrows foodborne illness slightly.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "frozen ice bricks", "the food that'll go off" for perishables, "as little as you can get away with", "your mitts", "Don't reuse marinade, full stop."

authenticity.evidence: Real Aussie voice: "a bloody field day for the bugs", "everyone's in and out of the drinks esky every five minutes", "Snags burnin' and the flies havin' a go".

tone.evidence: Friendly but firm safety advice: "That's not optional.", "Guessing doesn't count."

flow.evidence: Reads like it was written that way.

variety.evidence: Varied: "snags", "tucker", "esky", "ice bricks", "chook", "mitts", "cart it", "rocked up", "copping a blast".

problems.quote: a nasty dose of the runs
keep all your tongs, utensils and platters clean
problems.original: keep all utensils and platters clean

problems.quote: That keeps it warm without cooking it to a crisp.
problems.original: This keeps it hot but prevents overcooking.
problems.why: "warm" softens "hot", which matters for food safety.

B.summary: The most natural and complete version: varied, well-pitched and still clearly a safety guide.

meaning.evidence: Most guidelines kept verbatim, but "Meat, poultry, and seafood may be chockers while still frozen" garbles "may be packed" into "full", and the reader is called "ya flamin' mongrel".

sense.evidence: "chockers" (full) used for "packed"; "fronted up, ya flamin' mongrel" insults the reader; "tucker safety" for food safety.

authenticity.evidence: Stage-Australian: "Fair dinkum, to protect yourself", "Bugger me, Rinse fresh fruits", "Mind you, Marinate tucker in the refrigerator", "ay" bolted onto untouched FDA prose with US "refrigerator", "kitchen counter", "Organize".

register.evidence: Swearing within dad level, but mostly untranslated with bolted-on tags, well short of a level-4 retelling.

tone.evidence: A safety guide that abuses its reader ("ya flamin' mongrel") and exclaims "Bugger me" before rinsing fruit.

flow.evidence: Broken joins: "Bugger me, Rinse", "Mind you, Marinate", lower-case "tucker safety begins".

variety.evidence: "tucker" replaces nearly every "food", over twenty times.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the guide, but flattened and defaced by the tags.

problems.quote: Meat, poultry, and seafood may be chockers while still frozen
problems.original: Meat, poultry, and seafood may be packed while still frozen
problems.why: "chockers" means full; the instruction to pack frozen meat is garbled.

problems.quote: once you’ve fronted up, ya flamin' mongrel
problems.why: Added insult to the reader of a safety guide.

problems.quote: simple tucker safety guidelines for transporting your tucker
problems.original: simple food safety guidelines for transporting your food
problems.why: Representative of "tucker" swapped in for every "food".

C.summary: A word-swap pass with bolted-on tags and an insult; one instruction garbled.
